title: Today State: A System for Naming How You Feel Today
lead: Today State is a simple daily check-in system that lets you pick a few words describing where you are right now. Choose one or more states from each group to build a quick snapshot of your day, then share it with your team, your family, or just your future self. No scores and no judgment, only an honest label for today.

items.name: Flow (psychological state)
items.text: Flow is the state of full absorption in a challenging task, described by psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi. People are often surprised that it arises when skill and challenge are balanced, not when things feel easy. Many find it in sports, music, or focused work.

items.name: Circadian rhythm
items.text: The circadian rhythm is the body's roughly 24-hour internal clock that shapes alertness, sleep, and hormone release. Surprisingly, daylight is one of its strongest cues. Keeping regular wake times and getting morning light helps people feel steady through the day.

items.name: Caffeine
items.text: Caffeine is the world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance, found in coffee, tea, and cocoa. It works mainly by blocking adenosine, a chemical that builds sleepiness. Many people enjoy it as a morning ritual or a social break with colleagues.

items.name: Fatigue
items.text: Fatigue is a feeling of tiredness or lack of energy that rest does not always fix right away. It can be physical, mental, or both. People often manage it by noticing early signs, slowing down, and protecting their sleep.

items.name: Second wind
items.text: A second wind is the sudden return of energy after a period of exhaustion, a term first used for runners who regain breath and strength mid-race. Today people use it for any late burst of motivation, at work or play.

items.name: Nap (昼寝, hirune)
items.text: A nap is a short sleep during the day, often taken in the early afternoon. Many are surprised that even brief naps of about twenty minutes can improve alertness. Some workplaces and schools now encourage short rests to recharge.

items.name: Sunny (晴れ)
items.text: A bright, light mood when things simply feel good. Many people are surprised that naming a good day takes effort, since we rarely pause on it. Choosing Sunny lets you notice and enjoy it on purpose.

items.name: Calm (穏やか)
items.text: A steady, quiet state with little tension. It is often mistaken for boredom, but calm is a positive feeling in its own right. Picking Calm is a gentle reminder to protect an unhurried pace today.

items.name: Grateful (感謝)
items.text: A warm awareness of the people and things that support you. It can arise even on hard days, which surprises many. Naming it often leads people to thank someone or jot down what they appreciate.

items.name: Excited (ワクワク)
items.text: High energy pointed toward something ahead, like an event, trip or new project. Its racing heart can feel much like nervousness. Choosing Excited helps you direct that energy into action instead of restlessness.

items.name: Cloudy (くもり)
items.text: A muted, low-key mood that is not clearly good or bad. People are often relieved that an in-between option exists. Naming Cloudy makes it easier to go gently and not force cheerfulness.

items.name: Irritable (イライラ)
items.text: A state where small things annoy you more than usual, often linked to tiredness, hunger or stress. Simply naming it can soften its grip. Choosing Irritable signals a need for rest, space or a short break.

items.name: Nostalgic (懐かしい)
items.text: A bittersweet longing for the past, often sparked by music, smells or old photos. It blends happiness and sadness at once. Picking Nostalgic invites you to revisit memories or reconnect with an old friend.

items.name: Hopeful (希望)
items.text: A forward-looking feeling that things can get better, even when today is not perfect. Hope can sit alongside worry, which surprises many. Choosing Hopeful encourages taking one small step toward what you want.

items.name: Deep Focus
items.text: A state of sustained, deliberate concentration on one demanding task. People are often surprised that it usually takes time to settle into and is easily broken. Many protect it with quiet spaces, silenced notifications and blocked-out time.

items.name: In the Zone (Flow)
items.text: Being fully absorbed in an activity, a state psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi called "flow." A surprise is how time seems to vanish. It tends to appear when a challenge closely matches your skill, as in sports, music or creative work.

items.name: Easily Distracted
items.text: A day when attention keeps drifting toward phones, noise or new thoughts. Many are surprised how common this is and how much sleep, stress and environment affect it. Naming it helps people choose lighter tasks or take short breaks.

items.name: Multitasking
items.text: Juggling several tasks or streams of information at once. Research surprises many people: the brain usually switches rapidly between tasks rather than doing them simultaneously, which can cost time and accuracy. It suits routine, low-stakes work best.

items.name: Brain Fog
items.text: An informal term for feeling mentally cloudy, slow or forgetful. It is not a medical diagnosis itself but a description of symptoms linked to things like poor sleep, illness or stress. Naming it invites gentleness and rest.

items.name: Daydreaming
items.text: Letting the mind wander into imagined scenes, plans or memories while awake. Surprisingly, mind-wandering occupies a large share of waking thought and is linked to creativity and planning. Many enjoy it on walks, commutes or quiet afternoons.

items.name: Restful Sleep
items.text: Feeling well rested follows enough good-quality sleep, letting body and mind recover. Many people are surprised that sleep consolidates memory, not just energy. Logging this state helps you notice which bedtime routines actually leave you refreshed.

items.name: Sleepiness (Somnolence)
items.text: Sleepiness is the strong urge to sleep, driven by built-up sleep pressure and the body's circadian rhythm. Surprisingly, a dip in alertness after lunch is normal for many people. Naming it helps you plan breaks or a short nap.

items.name: Hunger
items.text: Hunger is the body's signal that it needs food, shaped partly by hormones such as ghrelin. People are often surprised that thirst or tiredness can feel like hunger. Tracking it shows how meal timing affects your mood.

items.name: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness (DOMS)
items.text: This is the aching that appears after unfamiliar or intense exercise. Surprisingly, it usually peaks one to three days later rather than right away. Recording it helps you balance workouts with gentle movement and recovery.

items.name: Malaise
items.text: Feeling under the weather describes general discomfort or unease, often an early sign of illness like a cold. The idiom is commonly said to have nautical origins. Naming it early is a reminder to rest and look after yourself.

items.name: Runner's High
items.text: After exercise, many people feel uplifted, calm, or energized. Researchers link this to brain chemicals including endorphins and endocannabinoids, and it is not limited to running. Logging it shows how much movement brightens the rest of your day.

items.name: Chatty
items.text: A state that tells others you welcome conversation today. People are often surprised how much a simple signal lowers the barrier to saying hello. Friends and coworkers use it as an open invitation for small talk, quick check-ins, or catching up.

items.name: Quiet Mode
items.text: A gentle way to say you are present but prefer fewer words today. Many find it freeing to set this without needing to explain. Others respond by keeping messages short and kind, respecting a calmer pace without assuming anything is wrong.

items.name: Open to Collaborate
items.text: Signals that you have energy and time to work with others on ideas or tasks. It surprises people how often it sparks unexpected partnerships. Teammates use it to find willing helpers, brainstorm together, or pair up on shared projects.

items.name: Do Not Disturb
items.text: Borrowed from the familiar hotel door sign and phone setting, this state marks focused or private time. People appreciate that it sets a boundary politely. Others save non-urgent messages for later, trusting you will reconnect when you are ready.

items.name: Needs a Hug
items.text: A soft way to let trusted people know you could use some comfort or encouragement today. Many are surprised how naming the need makes support easier to give. Friends often respond with a kind message, a check-in, or a real hug.

items.name: Party Ready
items.text: Shows you are in a festive mood and up for fun, gatherings, or spontaneous plans. People are often delighted by how quickly it brings like-minded friends together. It is commonly used to organize meetups, celebrations, or an evening out.

items.name: Light Day
items.text: A Today State for days with few commitments and open space in the schedule. Many people are surprised that naming a quiet day helps them use it well, whether for rest, deep thinking, or small tasks.

items.name: Busy but Fine
items.text: A Today State for full days that still feel manageable. It separates being busy from being stressed, which many people find surprisingly freeing. Sharing it tells teammates you are occupied but still reachable and doing well.

items.name: Deadline Mode
items.text: A Today State for focusing on one deadline that matters most. Many people are surprised how much this label reduces interruptions. Others read it as a polite signal to hold non-urgent questions until the work is delivered.

items.name: Overloaded
items.text: A Today State for days when demands go beyond what one person can reasonably handle. Saying it plainly can feel hard at first, but it often invites help, lets you reset priorities, and prevents quiet burnout before it grows.

items.name: Catching Up
items.text: A Today State for clearing a backlog after time away, illness, or a hectic stretch. Many people find relief in admitting they are behind. It sets realistic expectations while you work through messages, tasks, and pending replies.

items.name: Wrapping Up
items.text: A Today State for finishing projects, handing off work, or closing out a week. It surprises people how satisfying it is to name an ending. Colleagues know it is a good moment for final reviews and loose ends.

items.name: Clear Skies
items.text: A calm, bright day when your mind feels open and focused. Many people are surprised how rarely they notice this state while it lasts. Naming it helps you enjoy it fully and remember what helped it happen.

items.name: Gentle Breeze
items.text: A light, easygoing mood with a little movement in it: mildly curious, a bit restless, but comfortable. People often mistake it for distraction. Treat it as a good time for walks, small tasks, and casual conversations.

items.name: Foggy Morning
items.text: A hazy state when thoughts feel slow and unclear, often after poor sleep or a busy stretch. It can come without any real problem behind it. Naming it lets you lower expectations kindly and wait for it to lift.

items.name: Passing Storm
items.text: A day of strong feelings such as frustration, sadness, or worry. Calling it 'passing' is a reminder that intense emotions usually shift with time. Naming it lets others give you space without needing a long explanation.

items.name: Rainbow After Rain
items.text: The relief and soft brightness that follows a hard time. People are often surprised that difficult days can make this feeling sharper. It is a good moment to thank people who helped and notice what changed.

items.name: Starry Night
items.text: A quiet, reflective mood, often in the evening, when you feel thoughtful rather than active. It can feel lonely or peaceful, sometimes both. Many use it for journaling, gentle music, or simply resting without a plan.
